questions.q: What are the two real rollback strategies this lesson covers?
options: Reverting to the exact prior state, or rolling forward with a targeted fix
Deleting the application entirely, or ignoring the issue until the next release
Always reverting, since rolling forward is never a legitimate option
Always rolling forward, since reverting is never a legitimate option
questions.explain: Neither strategy is automatically correct — the right call depends on what actually broke and how it was built.

questions.q: Why is a clean revert described as powerful in this lesson?
options: It restores a state the team already knows worked, with no guesswork about whether the result is correct
It is always faster than writing a roll-forward fix
It automatically identifies the root cause of the problem
It requires no prior version history or commit history to work
questions.explain: A revert's strength is certainty — the restored version was already running successfully a moment before the deployment.

questions.q: When is rolling forward the better call, per this lesson?
options: Whenever the issue is catastrophic and affects every user, regardless of fix readiness
When the root cause is already understood, the fix is small and low-risk, and reverting would discard other working functionality from the same deployment
Only when source control is unavailable
Never — reverting is always the safer and faster choice
questions.explain: Roll-forward wins when the fix is narrow, well understood, and a full revert would cost more than it saves.

questions.q: Why can a messy, partially-applied deployment be HARDER to cleanly revert than to simply fix forward?
options: Reverting a scattered deployment risks undoing other things that are working correctly, or failing to fully back out everything that changed
Messy deployments cannot be reverted under any circumstances
A messy deployment always has fewer dependencies than a clean one
Reverting a messy deployment is always instant regardless of how it was built
questions.explain: This echoes Chapter 2's lesson on overly broad Update Sets — unrelated changes welded together make a clean, surgical undo difficult.

questions.q: What three real questions drive the revert-vs-roll-forward decision, according to this lesson?
options: How bad and widespread the issue is, how fast a roll-forward fix can realistically be tested, and how cleanly the deployment could actually be reverted
Which developer wrote the original code, what time zone the team is in, and how long the pipeline took to run
Only the number of lines of code changed in the deployment
Whether the CAB has already met, regardless of the issue itself
questions.explain: Severity and scope, roll-forward speed and confidence, and revert cleanliness are the three real decision criteria this lesson describes.
